papers.title: Making sense of wildfire prevention in the southwestern United States: Workforce perspectives on organizational challenges in federal land management agencies
papers.abstract: Abstract Wildfire prevention yields a high return on investment, yet research suggests that efforts to modernize prevention resources, programs, and funding within U.S. federal land management agencies are scarce despite rising ignition risk. Investigating the experiences and needs of fire prevention staff tasked with undertaking risk reduction while interacting with a rapidly diversifying portfolio of public land users, including current challenges and opportunities that would benefit from additional support, is critical for advancing holistic wildfire adaptation on public lands. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 31 federal agency employees for whom fire prevention was a primary job responsibility in the U.S. states of Arizona and New Mexico to document the current state of fire prevention in federal land management agencies. Interviews uncovered three core challenges: a lack of clarity about what prevention entails and its role within federal agencies, inability to demonstrate prevention “success,” and a lack of capacity for innovation. Promotion opportunities under these constraints were limited, resulting in a wildfire prevention ‘brain drain’ to other agencies or regions of the U.S. that retention of local knowledge not yet captured by data or decision support tools. These systemic and localized barriers motivated interest in a more defined balance between position responsibilities and role flexibility. We use organizational sensemaking and sensegiving as a theoretical lens to provide actionable insights for agency decision makers, emphasizing a need for strategic resource coordination and greater clarity surrounding what prevention entails to demonstrate programmatic value and encourage collective action.

papers.title: Prescribed burning and post-fire recovery time shape microhymenopteran communities in high-nature-value grasslands
papers.abstract: Semi-natural dry grasslands of Central Europe represent important biodiversity hotspots but are increasingly affected by land-use change and restoration management practices, including prescribed burning. Although fire is applied to maintain open grassland structure, its effects on microhymenopterans remain poorly understood. We investigated the responses of microhymenoptera assemblages to contrasting fire regimes in xerothermic grasslands. We compared abandoned unburned sites with sites exposed to prescribed burning differing in frequency and time since fire. Sampling was conducted using Malaise traps from April to July 2024 across nine localities. In total, 3,975 specimens representing six superfamilies and several families of the Chalcidoidea superfamily were analysed using generalized linear mixed models. Microhymenoptera abundance was generally highest in unburned control sites, indicating that long-term abandonment provides relatively stable and resource-rich conditions. However, sites sampled one year after fire showed a temporary increase in abundance, suggesting a short-term positive response during early post-fire succession. In contrast, sites sampled shortly after the most recent burn, whether burned once or in successive years showed significantly reduced abundance across several dominant groups, particularly Chalcidoidea and within it Mymaridae and Aphelinidae. Seasonality strongly influenced microhymenoptera dynamics, with abundance consistently declining from spring to mid-summer across all management regimes. Our results demonstrate that the ecological effects of prescribed burning on microhymenoptera communities are strongly influenced by fire frequency. While burning followed by at least one full growing season of undisturbed recovery may enhance abundance through opened vegetation structure and post-fire recolonisation, short intervals between successive burns appear detrimental to microhymenopteran populations. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining a heterogeneous mosaic of burned and unburned habitats for biodiversity conservation in species-rich xerothermic grasslands.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal wildfire occurrence, burn severity and early post-fire vegetation recovery in a tropical Andean landscape: Quilanga, southern Ecuador
papers.abstract: Wildfires are recurrent environmental hazards in tropical Andean landscapes, where limited spatial records can constrain prevention, impact assessment, and post-fire management. This study presents an integrated assessment to characterize wildfire occurrence, burn severity, and early vegetation-greenness recovery in Quilanga, southern Ecuador. Official wildfire records from 2010-2025 were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Mann-Kendall tests, Sen’s slopes, and multiscale kernel density estimation. August 2024 wildfire was assessed using Sentinel-2-derived NBR and dNBR, a land-use and land-cover map, MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections, and geocoded locality level impact reports. Post-fire spectral greenness response was evaluated using NDVI observations acquired before, immediately after, approximately one year after, and nearly two years after the event. A total of 107 reported wildfire records and 18,486 ha of reported burned vegetation area were recorded. Cumulative monthly wildfire activity was concentrated primarily between August and October, with September presenting the highest cumulative frequency and reported burned area. Annual reported wildfire frequency and reported burned vegetation area both showed statistically significant positive trends. Multiscale KDE identified a north-central concentration of reported occurrences, which remained comparatively consistent across bandwidths and after conservative record consolidation, although the extent of high-density zones varied with bandwidth. The dNBR-derived affected area covered 6,866ha, compared with the 6,295 ha of burned vegetation reported by SNGR, and showed ancillary spatial consistency with 77.4% of MODIS and 83.8% of VIIRS active-fire detections, as well as with reported affected localities. Non-forest natural vegetation contained the largest fire-affected area and the greatest absolute extent of moderate and high spectral severity. The integration of operational records, multisensor imagery, LULC data, and complementary contextual evidence provide a reproducible assessment approach for wildfire characterization and post-fire monitoring in data-constrained regions.

papers.title: Fire danger and wildfire occurrence in Botswana’s savannas: evaluating fire-danger indices and early-warning thresholds using 2001–2024 observations
papers.abstract: Abstract. Fire danger indices are important tools for operational fire management, yet their performance in African savannas remains poorly evaluated. We assessed eight widely used indices, Fine Fuel Moisture Code (FFMC), Forest Fire Weather Index (FWI), McArthur Forest Fire Danger Index (FFDI), Initial Spread Index (ISI), Drought Moisture Code (DMC), Buildup Index (BUI), Drought Code (DC), and Keetch–Byram Drought Index (KBDI) against 24 years (2001–2024) of Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) derived fire occurrence data across Botswana. Index values were calculated from ERA5 Land reanalysis data and evaluated using Spearman rank correlation, logistic regression with cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and percentile-based odds ratios across annual, dry-season, and wet-season periods. Fine fuel moisture indices consistently outperformed deep drought codes. FFMC showed the strongest discrimination (AUC = 0.821; P90 OR = 9.08), followed by FFDI, FWI, and ISI, whereas DC and KBDI ranked lowest. Fire occurrence odds were approximately seven to nine times higher at or above the 90th percentile than below the threshold, with the steepest increases occurring above approximately the 70th–75th percentile range. No index was significantly correlated with seasonal fire totals (ρ < 0.22, p > 0.05), indicating that these indices are better suited to assessing daily fire danger than cumulative seasonal activity. The findings support a fire danger monitoring framework for Botswana in which FFMC serves as the primary daily indicator, supported by FFDI and FWI, with alert thresholds anchored to the 75th and 90th percentiles of a locally derived climatology.

papers.title: Multilevel regression trees with application to wildfires in the American west
papers.abstract: We propose a Bayesian regression tree model fit within a multilevel structure and apply it to historic wildfire data in the western United States. Sharing of information between related groups (ecoregions) combined with highly interpretable regression trees allows for better predictions and understanding of climate and land cover variables predictive of wildfires. By doing a simulation study with a range of performance metrics, we demonstrate our method produces tree posteriors most structurally similar to assumed true trees, while simultaneously achieving good out-of-sample predictive performance. Applied to a large wildfire data set, we explore variable splits within regression trees corresponding to each ecoregion in detail, taking into account known features of each location. Shared hyperparameters between trees provide highly useful understanding of both variable and split value importance in predicting wildfires among all ecoregions, with no direct parallel in comparable models. Namely, we highlight potential evaporation, temperature, and evergreen forest land cover as variables most associated with historic wildfires, with some observable patterns in split values most commonly chosen across the groups. We propose a new algorithm based on parallel tempering, conditioning on shared hyperparameters at the true posterior temperature, improving Markov chain mixing, a known bottleneck in Bayesian CART models.

papers.title: A method for characterising fire events in high fire frequency landscapes: case study application to North Kimberley fire regimes, Western Australia
papers.abstract: Background Identifying fire events provides insights into fire size distribution, the timing of significant fire events, their behaviour and ignition causes. However, this can be challenging when using temporally coarse datasets across high-fire-frequency savanna landscapes. Aims Develop and validate a fire event delineation (FED) methodology. Methods We introduce a fire size distribution (FSD) method combining high-resolution burnt area mapping with high temporal resolution hotspot data to produce detailed day-of-burn attributed mapping. This approach is applied to 2014–2023 fire mapping of North Kimberley savannas, northern Australia. Key results Analysis of the ten largest fires per year (n = 100) indicated their responsibility for 33.3% of total area burnt annually, with 69% occurring during the late dry season. Additionally, only 35% of these fires started in locations with on-ground access. Remote ignition fires burnt 51 and 64% of total area with all land burnt late in the year, respectively. A ~50% decrease in large fire sizes was observed, due to improved intensive fuel management. Conclusions The FED method provided an easily implementable and useful new approach for understanding fire regimes in high fire frequency landscapes. Implications Previous FSD methods underestimated total fire size for fires burning over multiple months. The method presented here improves on previous approaches.

papers.title: Record-breaking wildfire intensity and nocturnal spread during the extreme 2025 wildfire season in Southwestern Europe: causes and impacts
papers.abstract: Europe faced an extreme wildfire season in 2025, with nearly 700,000 ha burned in the Iberian Peninsula (IP) alone. Here, we analyze the drivers and impacts of the 2025 wildfire season in the IP and its significance within the ongoing global pyrocrisis. Decades-long declines in burned area, driven by increased fire suppression, appear to be changing after an inflection point in 2022. Fire intensity has escalated over the last two decades, and estimated fire radiative energy in 2025 approached the annual output of a 1,000 MW nuclear reactor. Despite an unusually wet spring, an extreme summer heatwave triggered a flash drought, dehydrating fuels below critical thresholds. Remarkably, 29-42% of all analyzed wildfires spread faster at night than during the day, a seldom-reported phenomenon likely due to interactions between surface weather, atmospheric instability and, potentially, pyroconvection. Increases in fire intensity likely facilitated the overwhelming of suppression efforts during simultaneous fire events that may have been manageable decades ago. Wildfires expanded into previously fire-free high-altitude regions, and fire-size distributions changed markedly, including the largest wildfire in record and the highest proportion of burned area by fires exceeding 5,000ha. Impacts included 1595-2291 estimated premature deaths from smoke exposure and significant effects on protected areas. Initial rates of fire spread varied substantially across fuel models, indicating the importance of land management. These results reveal shifts in key components of fire regimes, including unprecedented nocturnal fire acceleration and fire intensity, with escalating impacts on human health and ecosystems where fuel management remains the main option to curb increasing fire intensity.

papers.title: Sulfur Dioxide Point Sources Remain Important for Daytime Plume‐Scale New Particle Formation in the United States: Case Study for Gary, Indiana During the Summer 2023 AEROMMA Aircraft Campaign
papers.abstract: Abstract Plumes from sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) point sources have been shown to be significant contributors to new particle formation (NPF), but SO 2 emissions in the United States (US) have decreased drastically by ∼10× since the early 2000s. We present observations of plume‐scale NPF from SO 2 point sources over the industrial hub in Gary, Indiana and assess the importance of SO 2 plumes to NPF using the P6 subgrid NPF parameterization and model the subsequent aerosol growth using the Statistical Oxidation Model‐TwO Moment Aerosol Sectional (SOM‐TOMAS) kinetic gas/aerosol model. We identify 29 SO 2 ‐rich NPF plumes downwind of SO 2 point sources in our observations. Across eight separate flight passes over Gary, the total plume‐scale particle production rate via NPF is estimated to be in the range of 8.5 × 10 13 –3.5 × 10 18 # s −1 and is typically comparable to or greater than primary particle number emissions from traffic in nearby Chicago. On a single case day, subsequent growth of newly formed particles is mainly driven by regional condensation of organics and coagulation. These results demonstrate the continued importance of SO 2 point sources for plume‐scale NPF and regional aerosol number concentrations, including those of climate‐relevant sizes (<50–100 nm diameter), despite more than a factor‐of‐10 reduction in SO 2 emissions in recent decades. Further, organics are critical in sustaining the growth of these newly formed particles, and organics may be more important for this growth compared to past decades due to reduced sulfuric acid (H 2 SO 4 ).

papers.title: Right on time: evaluating accuracy and timing of burn-severity assessments to support post-fire management
papers.abstract: Abstract Effective wildfire impact assessment and post-fire management rely on burn-severity maps that accurately characterize fire effects on vegetation and soils. These maps inform time-sensitive activities such as post-fire flood and debris-flow modeling, risk mitigation for homes and communities, and ecosystem recovery planning, but the satellite observations used to generate them are often obstructed or delayed by smoke, clouds, and snow. Across 9,129 large fires (≥ 404 ha) in Canada and the United States from 2016–2024, we quantified post-fire data obstruction and evaluated observational latency – defined as the time required to acquire the first usable scene – for four freely available moderate-resolution remote sensing datasets: Landsat, Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) product. For multispectral datasets (Landsat, Sentinel-2, and HLS), cloud cover was the primary source of data obstruction, particularly in mesic and coastal regions, whereas Sentinel-1 (synthetic aperture radar) can penetrate clouds. Consequently, Sentinel-1 had the shortest observational latency (median = 4 days), followed by HLS (7 days), Sentinel-2 (10 days), and Landsat (17 days). Likewise, one-month composite imagery from Sentinel-1 (89.6%) and HLS (82.8%) achieved near-complete coverage for most fires, substantially better than Sentinel-2 (70.5%) and Landsat (56.1%). Despite its widespread use in operational burn-severity mapping, Landsat provided the slowest and least complete early post-fire coverage. For 77 fires in forested ecosystems, we also evaluated relationships between early post-fire imagery and field-derived burn-severity measurements collected 0–3 years after fire. All multispectral datasets corresponded well with field data and reliably identified areas of near-total canopy loss using imagery acquired within two months after fire (> 80% balanced accuracy), performing nearly as well as extended assessments using imagery from a full post-fire growing season. Sentinel-1 produced less accurate burn-severity estimates but may remain valuable where persistent cloud cover limits observations, including eastern Canada and the Pacific Northwest. Overall, HLS provided the best combination of latency, spatial coverage, and burn-severity mapping performance, making it a strong candidate for operational use and ecological monitoring across diverse North American ecosystems.

papers.title: Playing with fire: Wolf response to active wildfires, fire fronts and smoke
papers.abstract: Wildfires are a key natural disturbance in fire-prone ecosystems, but their impacts on wildlife are increasingly significant as fire regimes intensify globally. Although considerable research has examined animal responses to post-wildfire landscapes, little is known about how animals respond to burning fires. While fires often trigger avoidance behaviours, predators may benefit from fire-related hunting opportunities. We present one of the first studies, to our knowledge, explicitly examining fine-scale behavioural responses of a large carnivore to actively burning wildfires, testing whether predators balance the potential risks and benefits associated with these dynamic disturbances. Using integrated step selection analysis, we assessed how wolves respond to active fires (burning areas with flaming or smouldering combustion, and recently extinguished burns), fire fronts (areas with flaming combustion) and smoke in a North American boreal forest. We asked: (i) Do wolves select or avoid active fires, fire fronts, or smoke, or alter their movement rates in response to these disturbances? and (ii) Do active fires, fire fronts or smoke alter wolf selection of habitat? Wolves selected for areas near active fires, particularly longer-lasting ones, but avoided fire fronts, potentially balancing risk avoidance with fire-related predation opportunities. Further, wolves altered their habitat use in ways that offset fire-related risks, including moving faster in smokier conditions and selecting for water and polygonal anthropogenic disturbances near active fires and in smoky areas. Our novel findings on predator behaviours during wildfires highlight the nuanced relationships between predation opportunities and risk avoidance, with implications for predator-prey dynamics in fire-prone regions experiencing increasing wildfire severity, frequency and scale.

papers.title: Molecular Evidence for the Atmospheric Transformation of Trash Burning Aerosol Into Organonitrate‐ and Organosulfate‐Rich Haze: A Case Study From the Eastern Indo‐Gangetic Plain
papers.abstract: Abstract Open burning of solid waste is projected to contribute up to 29% of global anthropogenic PM 2.5 emissions, yet its role in secondary aerosol formation remains largely absent from current assessments. The downwind ambient aerosol in haze was dominated by less volatile, highly oxygenated organonitrates and organosulfates (>85% of the formulae), consistent with substantial atmospheric transformation. Single‐particle measurements show that freshly emitted tbOA is internally mixed with inorganic salts, implying enhanced hygroscopicity and aqueous‐phase processing as a mechanistic driver of this transformation. Our molecular‐level observations suggest a potential link between open trash burning and organonitrate‐ and organosulfate‐rich secondary aerosol in the regional winter boundary layer. Our results motivate targeted chamber experiments and regional modeling studies to better quantify the contributions and chemical evolution of trash burning emissions in air quality assessments.

papers.title: Interactive fires in the Canadian Earth System Model (Part 1): How wildfire characteristics change in the warming climate
papers.abstract: Wildland fires are increasingly important drivers of ecosystem change, air quality degradation, and climate feedbacks, yet their emissions and plume rise are commonly prescribed in Earth system models. Here we introduce interactive fire aerosol emissions and a thermodynamical plume-height parameterization into CanESM5.1c. We evaluate simulated area burned, black carbon (BC) emissions, plume heights, and atmospheric BC distributions against multiple observation-based datasets for 2000--2023, and assess future changes under low- and moderate-warming scenarios. CanESM5.1c simulates global area burned between GFED4 and GFED5 estimates, while BC fire emissions are slightly high. Simulated mean plume heights are about 0.8 km lower than satellite-derived estimates but capture their broad spatial variability. Relative to fixed climatological injection heights, interactive plume height increases atmospheric BC above 850 hPa by 5--10% and decreases near-surface BC by 5--20%. Under moderate warming, end-of-century area burned and BC fire emissions increase by 23% and 53% in the Arctic and 33% and 37% in northern mid-latitudes, respectively, while globally dominant tropical area burned and emissions decrease by 24% and 22%. The frequency of fire plumes exceeding 8 km in height increase in several regions, including Australia/New Zealand, and the northern boreal forests. These changes are consistent with regional shifts in fuel availability, soil moisture, lightning, and atmospheric stability. Extreme fires contribute disproportionately to regional BC emissions and become more frequent in many extra-tropical regions. Under low warming, many fire characteristics remain closer to present-day conditions, emphasizing the benefits of climate change mitigation.

papers.title: Economic impacts of complex disasters affecting seaports and their associated supply chains
papers.abstract: We develop a multi-regional computable general equilibrium (CGE) modeling approach to assess both direct and cascading supply-chain effects of complex seaport disruptions across U.S. regions and sectors. The analysis introduces a new, internally consistent method for estimating ship offloading congestion and the resilience effects of ship rerouting within the model’s production and trade structure. The model is illustrated by analyzing economic impacts of a complex seaport disruption involving a labor strike, wildfire-induced power outage, and terrorist attack at the twin ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, the largest container port system in the United States. Results show that overlapping disruptions amplify losses well beyond the sum of individual events, with regional GDP in the Los Angeles Metropolitan area declining by $4.1 billion (0.37%) under our base case. Moreover, national-level impacts are substantially lower than the port region impacts because other regions of the country pick up a good deal of the slack of lost production in LA Metro. Incorporating resilience tactics, such as ship rerouting, excess capacity, inventories, and production recapture, reduces the port region losses by over 70%. These findings demonstrate that complex disruptions can lead to wide-ranging indirect economic effects, emphasizing the importance of integrating resilience into infrastructure investment, port operations, and national freight policy. In particular, enhancing inter-port coordination, increasing on-site electricity capacity, strengthening management effectiveness, and embedding resilience metrics into government programs can help reduce cascading risks and improve long-term economic stability.

papers.title: Policy and cost analysis for biochar development: a global review and Northeast US case study
papers.abstract: Abstract Biochar is a carbon-rich material created through the pyrolysis of organic biomass, offering multiple environmental benefits for soil improvement and climate change mitigation. While its use is expected to grow, particularly in the Northeast United States, widespread adoption faces challenges, including social distrust, economic hurdles, and high production costs. This study uses a structured narrative review of global policies to identify instruments such as financial, nonfinancial, and research & development that could inform decision-makers on biochar policy. We also developed a techno-economic breakeven model to quantify the impact of policies like input subsidies and tax credits on production costs in the Northeast United States. Our analysis shows that high production and entry costs require strategic policy interventions, including market-creation policies and regulatory clarity for feedstock procurement. Global examples showcase varied successful strategies, ranging from Australia’s carbon credit systems to Japan’s R&D support. We recommend that the Northeast US establish scientific certainty and trust, foster a regional network with Canada, and implement multi-instrument strategies that combine incentives, regulatory adjustments, and continued R&D to drive large-scale commercialization. These findings provide a roadmap for policy makers to help biochar reach its full potential in the region.

papers.title: Drivers of individual-tree mortality in Picea abies and Pinus sylvestris: A large-scale analysis across Austria
papers.abstract: Understanding the drivers of tree mortality is essential for developing proactive management strategies to mitigate forest decline under climate change. However, empirical individual-tree mortality models parameterized with long-term inventory and climatic data remain scarce. Results reveal distinct, species-specific vulnerabilities to stand structure and climatic stressors. Both species are strongly driven by diameter at breast height (DBH), basal area of larger trees (BAL), and warm spring mean temperatures. Spruce is additionally sensitive to high summer maximum temperatures and exceptionally wet, stagnant summer conditions. Vapour pressure deficits (VPD) interacted with soil groups show no effect on either species, except for spruce on planosols and stagnic gleysols on loess. Notably, spruce benefits from warmer long- baseline temperatures across montane and lowland elevation zones—indicating vulnerability to weather volatility rather than thermal baseline warming—whereas Scots pine crosses its physiological threshold in chronically warmer lowlands. Admixtures also drive patterns: spruce mortality probability increase when mixed with European beech ( Fagus sylvatica ) and decrease when mixed with light-demanding conifers, whereas pine vulnerability rises when mixed with broadleaves or spruce. This divergence underscores the superior resilience of Scots pine to episodic climatic shocks, contrasted against a precarious state for Norway spruce, where minor climatic deviations trigger substantial mortality.

papers.title: Open Waste Burning in Indonesia: Pulmonary Toxicity, Injury Mechanisms, and Clinical Challenges
papers.abstract: Open waste burning is a widespread but underrecognized source of air pollution, particularly where waste services are inadequate. This narrative review aimed to synthesize evidence on the scale and drivers of open waste burning, emission toxicology, mechanisms of lung injury, respiratory effects, clinical management, and public-health implications, with relevance to Indonesia. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and relevant institutional sources were searched. Evidence was classified into three tiers: direct waste-burning evidence, analogous combustion-exposure evidence, and broader air-pollution evidence. Open waste burning releases particulate matter, black carbon, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, volatile organic compounds, metals, dioxins, and furans, which may promote oxidative stress, epithelial barrier dysfunction, impaired mucociliary defense, immune activation, and airway remodeling. Available evidence indicates potential acute respiratory symptoms and exacerbation of existing respiratory disease, although direct epidemiological evidence remains limited. No exposure-specific biomarker or treatment protocol has been established. Clinical management should therefore emphasize exposure history, syndrome-based care, and exposure reduction, while public-health measures should prioritize improved waste services and source control. The review is limited by heterogeneous evidence and the scarcity of exposure-linked human studies. Prospective studies are needed to quantify respiratory burden and evaluate intervention benefits.

papers.title: Land use and land cover change in the Okavango Delta, Botswana: integrating remote sensing and community perspectives on change drivers
papers.abstract: Land use and land cover change is a complex process triggered by either natural or anthropogenic factors. It has important implications for socioeconomic development and environmental sustainability. The present study assessed the dynamics of LULC in Shakawe and Gumare villages of northern Botswana from 1990 to 2023. The study also analysed stakeholders’ perceptions regarding the causes of LULC transformations. The drivers and patterns of land use and land cover change (LULCC) were identified by adopting satellite imagery analysis and a survey approach. The study employed supervised digital image classification and change detection techniques in combination with structured surveys to capture stakeholders’ perceptions. The results show urbanisation and agriculture are the dominant drivers of LULCC, leading to notable alterations in built-up areas, vegetation cover, and infrastructure development. The framework includes suggestions for long-term monitoring of bee behaviour, species richness, abundance and distributions using a variety of methods to capture information across species, locations and seasons. We advocate for continued and enhanced engagement with the public, who are already contributing to community science projects and online repositories. These findings suggest that the 2015 El Niño drought was associated with marked changes in water quality, particularly during the dry season, highlighting the sensitivity of Amazonian reservoirs to extreme climatic events.

papers.title: Ranking the wrong places: vulnerability assessment, flood losses and risk sharing in Italy and Europe
papers.abstract: Before a flood, governments decide where to invest in protection; after it, how much of the loss to compensate. The European Union informs the first decision with a composite index that ranks every subnational unit by vulnerability. This paper tests the ranking by comparing Italian provinces struck by the same flood between 2005 and 2024. The published index does not order provinces by the losses they suffer, with or without controls for hazard, exposure and income ($ρ$ between -0.06 and 0.09). The failure lies in what it weights. As published, the index mostly measures economic development, while losses follow water: they arrive in recurring groups of provinces that share a river basin, and more than half of the ranking error lies between those groups. In a pre-registered test that rebuilds it and eight rivals at every forecast origin from 2010 to 2020, the index comes last on both questions an allocator asks. On where damage will land, its top ten provinces capture 16 per cent of later damage, less than a random draw; Italy's public flood hazard map, blind to losses, captures 44. On who loses more from the same water, its rank correlation with later losses is 0.03; its own components, reweighted on past losses, reach 0.42. Neither repair needs new data. The misranked loss is paid locally. Of EUR 12.3 billion recorded over 2013-2022, 85 per cent was not covered by national transfers, and prevention funding, scored the same way, does no better than chance. Because correlated losses cluster within borders, national pools in Europe need 39 per cent more reserve than cross-border pools of the same size. The index fails the same way across 1,142 European units, where the repairs are weaker.

papers.title: Associations of Outdoor Air Pollution With Cause-specific Mortality in Metastatic Prostate Cancer: A cohort study
papers.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular disease is an important competing cause of death in men with metastatic prostate cancer, and ambient air pollution may increase cardiovascular vulnerability. We evaluated associations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) with all-cause, cardiovascular, and prostate cancer-specific mortality, including joint associations with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). Methods: We analyzed 33,384 men from 11 US state registries diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer during 2000-2015 and followed through 2018. Residential PM2.5 and NO2 concentrations at diagnosis were assigned using 1-km exposure models. Multivariable Cox models estimated all-cause mortality, and inverse-probability-weighted Cox models assessed cause-specific mortality. Results: Each interquartile-range increase in PM2.5 was associated with higher cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.02-1.07; p-trend=0.008). Cardiovascular mortality was also higher in the fourth and fifth PM2.5 quintiles versus the first (HR 1.18 and 1.21, respectively). Higher NO2 was associated with prostate cancer-specific mortality in the highest quintile (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01-1.13). In joint analyses, ADT-treated men with high versus low PM2.5 exposure had higher cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.19, 95% CI 1.05-1.34), without clear evidence of effect modification (p-interaction=0.051). Conclusions: In men with metastatic prostate cancer, higher PM2.5 exposure was associated with cardiovascular mortality, particularly among ADT-treated patients, supporting further study of environmental exposures and systemic therapy in cardio-oncology.

papers.title: Place-based climate adaptation: How Atlantic Canadian communities translate local knowledge into action
papers.abstract: This study examines how communities in Atlantic Canada recognize, value, and integrate local knowledge into climate change adaptation, focusing on the enabling and constraining roles of funding, governance, and institutional structures. Guided by the Socio-Ecological Systems (SES) framework, the research forms part of a larger transdisciplinary project on collaborative governance in financing climate adaptation and mitigation. Using qualitative methods, including semi-structured interviews with municipal representatives, NGOs, funders, and community leaders, and participant observation, the study identifies both barriers and opportunities for embedding local knowledge in adaptation planning. Findings reveal that local knowledge is central to building climate resilience, not peripheral. Communities achieve the strongest climate action outcomes when flexible, multi-year funding is paired with supportive local policies, collaborative governance, and mechanisms for co-producing knowledge with technical experts. Successful examples emphasize grassroots project design, participatory governance, and place-based approaches tailored to community priorities. However, systemic barriers, including rigid, short-term funding programs, top-down policy frameworks, and bureaucratic institutional requirements, continue to limit the consistent and equitable use of local knowledge. From an SES perspective, the most effective adaptation strategies emerge from feedback loops between community experience, institutional support, and environmental change. The study concludes that policy shifts are needed to institutionalize long-term, locally controlled funding, formalize community participation in decision-making, and embed equity-centered, co-productive approaches into adaptation frameworks. Such measures would move beyond symbolic acknowledgment of local knowledge toward its substantive integration, ensuring climate action that is adaptive, context-specific, and grounded in the lived realities of Atlantic Canadian communities.

Several deep learning architectures, including CNN, RNN, LSTM, GRU, and BiLSTM, were implemented to capture nonlinear temporal dependencies in pollutant concentration patterns. Furthermore, a hybrid BiLSTM-GRU model was proposed to improve forecasting performance by integrating bidirectional sequence learning with efficient gated recurrent mechanisms. The predictive performance of all models was evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and coefficient of determination ( $$R^2$$ ). Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed Hybrid_BiLSTM_GRU model consistently outperformed the standalone models for all pollutants at both monitoring locations. At Noida Sector 62, the hybrid model achieved RMSE values of 41.01, 64.41, and 7.54 for PM $$_{2.5}$$ , PM $$_{10}$$ , and NO $$_2$$ , respectively, along with corresponding $$R^2$$ scores of 0.4846, 0.4280, and 0.6391. papers.title: From Narrative to Algorithm: A Risk Mechanism Theory Index for Urban Infrastructure Investment in Sub-Saharan Africa
papers.abstract: Rapidly expanding metropolitan areas across Sub-Saharan Africa face systemic risk from hazard-induced disruptions, exacerbated by infrastructure deficits and socioeconomic vulnerabilities. Traditional risk assessment frameworks frequently fail decision-makers by offering static, qualitative narratives that cannot prioritize capital allocation or track resilience over dynamic budget cycles. This paper presents the Risk Mechanism Theory Index (RMTI) framework, a single, decision-ready mathematical model, grounded in Risk Mechanism Design and Theory, and built to assess, quantify, and treat systemic risk across organizational, health, infrastructure, and urban contexts. Structurally, the RMTI reduces every risk environment to three correctly signed dimensions drawn from Table 9.4: RMTre (risk exposure, L · E), RMTseen (socio-economic and environmental vulnerability, V), and RMTrl (resilience capacity, ρ), combined into a single bounded 0–1 composite residual score R = L · Esel · V · (1−ρ). The RMTI is operationalized through a purpose-built calculator that automates the full computational pipeline and is complemented by a Python reference implementation (RMTI-Py) for registry-scale and pipeline use. Both modalities are validated end-to-end against three World Bank-profiled urban infrastructure cases in Sub-Saharan Africa (Bamako, Mali; Lagos, Nigeria; Lilongwe, Malawi) and benchmarked against three comparator cities (Nairobi, Kenya; Dar es Salaam, Tanzania; Lusaka, Zambia). Empirical results demonstrate that targeted $50 million capital investments reduce composite risk scores by 30.7% to 47.5%, systematically transitioning all three primary environments from Tier 4 (Severe) to Tier 3 (High). The framework provides a transparent, algorithmic pipeline for embedding risk-informed governance into capital-budgeting workflows across sectors, and is offered as a management decision-support tool for institutional investors, development banks, and municipal finance officers seeking a reproducible, data-analytic alternative to narrative-based risk reporting.

papers.title: “Nature” vs. Nature: An Analysis of the Nature Character in Two Creation Stories and Their Practical Implications
papers.abstract: Sacred stories are an entryway into societal attitudes, and so are worth examining in relation to the most pressing societal issues, including the climate crisis. This project contributes to the larger climate conversation by asking what the “Nature” character in the Christian and Algonquin Anishinaabeg creation stories tell us about the societies’ attitudes towards the natural environment. Drawing on narrative theory and thematic narrative analysis, the study investigates this question in the context of Ottawa, Canada, tracing the relationship between mythological frameworks, attitudes, and practical behaviour. The findings resist easy conclusions. Rather than confirming a straightforward relationship between myths and practice, the analysis reveals a more complex – and sometimes surprising – picture. What does emerge consistently is that the two creation stories encode a fundamental connection between human and other-than-human nature – a connection that contemporary Canadian society may have lost sight of. The broader implication is urgent: if we are willing to read our creation stories closely and to interrogate our assumptions about them, they may provide a pathway for rethinking our environmental attitudes. At a moment of ecological crisis, this may be not merely illuminating, but necessary for our survival.

papers.title: ASAS-NANP SYMPOSIUM: MATHEMATICAL MODELING IN ANIMAL NUTRITION: Model Transfer and Application in Livestock Production Systems
papers.abstract: Mathematical models have long supported nutrition management in livestock systems, progressing from early National Research Council empirical tables to complex mechanistic frameworks such as the Ruminant Nutrition System. What is less documented is how models are operationalized in commercial practice, particularly as data streams from precision livestock technologies, remote sensing, and other Internet of Things technologies are increasingly hybridized into existing modeling frameworks. A prevailing assumption is that greater sensing, automation, or algorithmic complexity will naturally translate into better decisions; however, adoption and impact in commercial systems remain uneven. To examine how models are actually used under real-world constraints, we conducted a literature review and semi-structured interviews (n = 11) with livestock producers, technology developers, consultants, and value-chain actors working at the interface of biology, data, models, and farm decision-making. Six cross-cutting themes emerged: 1) model augmentation of systems, 2) model predictive control (MPC), 3) human centered adoption, 4) technology fit, 5) data bottlenecks, and 6) data enlightened value chain (Figure 1). Collectively, these insights re-center nutrition as the integrating discipline for productivity, welfare, and sustainability, and emphasize MPC and open, interoperable data pipelines as prerequisites for moving beyond pilots toward durable adoption. Interviewees consistently emphasized that meaningful impact depends on aligning biological realism, software engineering, and value-chain incentives so that models support actionable decisions under commercial constraints, rather than pursuing automation for its own sake.

papers.title: The resilience dividend: A tractable climate-economy model
papers.abstract: This paper develops a quantitative, analytically tractable, closed-form climate-economic model to study mitigation and adaptation policies. We identify a “resilience dividend” under baseline scenarios, where avoided long-run climate damages substantially exceed the economic costs of moderate policy intervention. Conversely, delayed intervention imposes a dual burden: even aggressive late-stage abatement fails to counteract thermal and atmospheric inertia in the medium term, escalating cumulative costs, while inducing sustained temperature overshoot. When incorporating exogenous technological progress or quadratic climate damages, the model aligns with recent empirical evidence on catastrophic risks, demonstrating that highly stringent policy action transitions from a discretionary choice to an economic imperative. Finally, an extension incorporating the structural shift toward intangible capital reveals that digitalization alters long-term decarbonization pathways depending on whether dematerialization gains outweigh computational energy demand. Overall, the findings indicate that decisive, front-loaded climate policy serves as an indispensable foundation for long-term macroeconomic stability and prosperity.

papers.title: Redistributing Risk: Air-Quality Mortality under Two Stratospheric Aerosol Injection Strategies
papers.abstract: Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) could affect human health through multiple pathways, including changes to surface air quality, and the magnitude and sign of these impacts may depend on the injection strategy. This study compares the air-quality-related mortality effects of two SAI strategies, G6-1.5K-SAI (30°N and 30°S at ~21.5 km) and G6-1.5K-HiLLA (60°N and 60°S at ~15 km), in CESM2(WACCM6), both targeting a global mean temperature of 1.5°C above preindustrial levels under an SSP2-4.5 baseline. We use bias-corrected surface ozone and PM 2.5 concentrations alongside Global Burden of Disease exposure-response functions to estimate excess mortality from one ozone-related and seven PM 2.5 -related health outcomes under each strategy. Both strategies produce a hemispheric asymmetry in surface ozone, which increases across much of the Northern Hemisphere and decreases in the Southern Hemisphere, consistent with changes in stratosphere-troposphere exchange, UV-driven photochemistry, and reduced water vapor. Ozone-related mortality changes are latitudinally dependent but small and similar across strategies (~5,000-6,000 fewer deaths per year globally). PM 2.5 -related mortality responses, however, differ substantially between strategies. In the ensemble mean, G6-1.5K-SAI produces approximately 28,000 fewer deaths in global PM 2.5 mortality per year , while G6-1.5K-HiLLA produces approximately 74,000 additional deaths per year, with the difference associated primarily with enhanced dust production from changes in precipitation and wind patterns and greater exposure to sulfate aerosol under G6-1.5K-HiLLA. While SAI-driven changes in air-quality-related mortality are small in the context of the total projected burden under SSP2-4.5, these results demonstrate that, in CESM2(WACCM6), SAI strategies targeting the same global temperature can produce markedly different regional and global air-quality health outcomes.

papers.title: Reframing urban green infrastructure for particulate matter mitigation: a systematic review and functional planning framework for high-density cities
papers.abstract: Abstract Rapid urbanization and increasing particulate matter (PM) pollution have heightened public health risks in high-density urban environments, highlighting the need for effective nature-based solutions. Although urban green infrastructure (UGI) is widely recognized for its potential to improve air quality, existing classification systems, particularly those based on development purposes, remain inadequate for capturing the functional mechanisms necessary for effective PM mitigation. This limitation hinders the development of context-sensitive planning strategies that account for spatial conditions, emission sources, and human exposure. To address this gap, this study develops a PM-oriented functional planning framework for high-density cities by reclassifying UGI according to PM mitigation functions rather than conventional purpose-based categories. Drawing on 8 Korean institutional/policy documents and a systematic review of 139 academic studies (124 international and 15 Korean), four functional classification criteria, namely development purpose, proximity to emission sources, receptor vulnerability, and physical structure, were identified and used to establish an evidence-informed typology comprising ten PM-oriented UGI types. These types were contextualized and operationalized within the Korean urban system as a representative model for complex, high-density urban development. The findings indicate that type-specific strategies emphasizing deposition, blocking, and dispersion are essential for effective PM mitigation. Structurally diverse vegetation can enhance particle deposition in residential areas, whereas optimized vegetation porosity improves performance in roadside environments. The proposed framework offers a decision-support tool for policymakers and urban planners; however, further empirical validation is required to assess its effectiveness and applicability across diverse urban contexts.

papers.title: When environmental harm becomes cultural harm: The joint role of environmental identity and national-cultural identity in responses to threats to culturally meaningful landscapes
papers.abstract: Natural landscapes often carry culturally shared meanings, yet ecological harm is not always experienced as culturally threatening. The present research proposes a contextualized functional account of environmental identity: when natural landscapes are construed as culturally meaningful symbols of one’s nation, environmental identity makes the cultural implications of ecological harm psychologically salient, and national-cultural identity strengthens the expression of environmental identity in response to ecological harm. This account was supported across two studies. In Study 1 (cross-sectional; N = 300, Chinese sample), national-cultural identity moderated the relationship between environmental identity and responses to a real-world promotional campaign causing ecological harm to a culturally meaningful landscape (Mount Everest). Environmental identity was more strongly associated with perceived cultural impact, specific negative emotions, and negative evaluations of the associated brand at higher (vs. lower) levels of national-cultural identity. In Study 2 (experimental; N = 287, American sample), environmental identity showed stronger associations with perceived cultural impact and sadness in response to a fictitious brand campaign causing ecological harm to a culturally meaningful landscape (the Rocky Mountains) in the national-cultural identity (vs. neutral) condition. These findings highlight the joint role of environmental identity and national-cultural identity in response to ecological harm in culturally meaningful landscapes.

papers.title: Integrating mRMR and PSO–machine learning with SHAP interpretation for UAV-based maize aboveground biomass and carbon estimation
papers.abstract: Accurate estimation of crop aboveground biomass (AGB) and aboveground carbon (AGC) across growth stages is pivotal for evaluating agroecosystem carbon sequestration. Nevertheless, the integration of feature selection, model optimization, and interpretability for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based crop AGB estimation remains underexplored. We propose a comprehensive interpretable machine learning framework for whole-season crop AGB estimation. Maize was selected as the study crop, and multispectral UAV imagery was acquired at key growth stages. The minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR) algorithm was applied to screen spectral bands, vegetation indices (VIs), and texture features (TFs) to formulate various feature subsets. These subsets were coupled with three machine learning algorithms (random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and support vector regression (SVR)) optimized with particle swarm optimization (PSO) to develop stage-specific AGB prediction models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was used to determine the feature contributions. The optimal models were identified for AGB and AGC quantification. PSO-optimized RF with optimal feature combinations achieved the best AGB predictions [jointing: Bands+VIs+TFs; silking/maturity: Bands+VIs+TFs+plant height (PH)]. VIs such as the Normalized Near Infrared Index (NNIRI), the Normalized Difference Red Edge Index (NDRE), the Chlorophyll Index-Red Edge (CIreg), and the Chlorophyll Vegetation Index (CVI), along with the Red_Variance and PH, contributed significantly. AGB spatial distributions were mapped, and AGC was derived using carbon conversion coefficients. This framework provides a promising tool for crop carbon sequestration assessment and sustainable agricultural management.
